subject: maths
title: Comparing data sets
summary: Compare two data sets using centre and spread, read parallel dot plots and back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots, handle outliers and work backwards from a mean.
body:
Saying "our class did better" is easy — proving it with numbers is harder. Coaches compare players, scientists compare a treatment group with a control group, and shoppers compare delivery times before choosing a company. In each case you need to compare two whole **data sets**, not just two single numbers.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can compare two data sets using a measure of centre AND a measure of spread, read parallel dot plots and back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots, choose the fairest measure when there is an outlier, and work backwards from a mean.

## Before you start

This lesson builds on *Mean, median, mode and range (Year 7)* and *Displaying data (Year 7)*. You should be able to find the mean, median and range of a list, and read a dot plot and a stem-and-leaf plot.

**Warm-up**

1. Find the mean and median of 4, 9, 2, 7, 8. *(Answer: mean = 30 ÷ 5 = 6; in order 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, so median = 7)*
2. Find the range of 15, 3, 22, 9. *(Answer: 22 − 3 = 19)*

## Think of it like this

### Choosing between two buses

Bus A usually takes 20 minutes, but some days it takes 10 and some days 40. Bus B usually takes 22 minutes and is never more than 2 minutes early or late. If you have an exam, which do you catch? Most people choose Bus B — slightly slower on average, but you can **rely** on it. Comparing data sets is like this: you need the typical value (centre) AND how much it varies (spread).

*Where the analogy breaks down:* with buses you care about one trip; in statistics you are describing the whole group of values, and a bigger spread is not always "worse" — it just means less consistent.

## Key ideas

### Centre and spread — always both

A **measure of centre** (mean, median or mode) tells you a typical value. A **measure of spread** (here, the **range** = highest − lowest) tells you how much the values vary. Two data sets can have exactly the same centre but very different spreads, so a fair comparison always mentions both.

Mia and Zara each played 7 basketball games:

- Mia: 14, 16, 15, 13, 17, 15, 15
- Zara: 6, 24, 9, 22, 15, 21, 8

Both have mean = 105 ÷ 7 = 15 and median = 15. But Mia's range is 17 − 13 = 4 and Zara's is 24 − 6 = 18. Mia is far more **consistent**.

![Parallel dot plots of points scored in 7 games on a scale from 5 to 25. Mia's dots are bunched between 13 and 17 with three at 15. Zara's dots are spread out at 6, 8, 9, 15, 21, 22 and 24](/diagrams/y7/maths-advanced/comparing-data-sets-players.svg)

### Parallel dot plots

**Parallel dot plots** draw two dot plots one above the other on the **same scale**. Because the scale is shared you can see at a glance which group sits further right (larger values) and which group is more bunched up (smaller spread).

### Back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots

A **back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot** shares one stem down the middle. The leaves of one group go to the right, and the leaves of the other group go to the left. On the left side the leaves get bigger as you move **away** from the stem, so you read them from right to left.

### Outliers and the fairest centre

An **outlier** is a value far away from the rest. The mean uses every value, so one outlier can drag it a long way. The median only depends on the middle, so it hardly moves. The range uses the two extreme values, so an outlier makes it much bigger. When a set has an outlier, the median usually describes a typical value better than the mean.

### Groups of different sizes

If one class has 20 students and another has 28, compare their means or medians, not their totals — a bigger group will usually have a bigger total just because it has more people.

### Working backwards from the mean

Because mean = total ÷ number of values, you can always rebuild the total:

`total = mean × number of values`

This lets you find a missing value, or the score needed to reach a target mean.

### Writing a comparison

A good comparison sentence names both groups, the measure, the numbers and what it means in context, for example: "Mia and Zara have the same median (15 points), but Mia's range is 4 compared with Zara's 18, so Mia is much more consistent."

## Worked examples

### Example 1

Compare Mia's and Zara's scoring (data above).

Step 1: centre — both means are 105 ÷ 7 = 15 and both medians are 15, so on average they score the same.
Step 2: spread — Mia's range is 4, Zara's is 18.
Step 3: conclusion — "They score the same on average, but Mia is more consistent because her range (4) is much smaller than Zara's (18)."

### Example 2

Two classes sat the same test (marks out of 50).

| 7A leaves | Stem | 7B leaves |
|---|---|---|
| | 1 | 8 |
| 8 3 | 2 | 5 6 9 |
| 8 7 5 4 1 | 3 | 0 3 3 6 9 |
| 6 2 1 | 4 | 9 |

Key: 3 | 4 means 34 marks for 7B, and 1 | 3 means 31 marks for 7A.

Step 1: list 7A in order, reading the left leaves from the stem outwards: 23, 28, 31, 34, 35, 37, 38, 41, 42, 46 (10 marks).
Step 2: 7A median = average of the 5th and 6th marks = (35 + 37) ÷ 2 = **36**. Range = 46 − 23 = **23**.
Step 3: list 7B: 18, 25, 26, 29, 30, 33, 33, 36, 39, 49. Median = (30 + 33) ÷ 2 = **31.5**. Range = 49 − 18 = **31**.
Step 4: conclusion — 7A did better (median 36 compared with 31.5) and its marks were more consistent (range 23 compared with 31).

### Example 3

Waiting times (minutes) at two cafés: Café A: 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 26. Café B: 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 6. Which café is quicker on a typical day?

![Parallel dot plots of waiting times from 0 to 30 minutes. Café A has dots at 3, 4, 4, 5 and 6 and one far away at 26. Café B has two dots each at 6, 7 and 8](/diagrams/y7/maths-advanced/comparing-data-sets-cafes.svg)

Step 1: means — A: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 minutes; B: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 minutes. The means say B is quicker.
Step 2: medians — A: (4 + 5) ÷ 2 = 4.5 minutes; B: in order 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, so (7 + 7) ÷ 2 = 7 minutes. The medians say A is quicker.
Step 3: why they disagree — 26 is an outlier that drags A's mean up. Without it, A's mean is 22 ÷ 5 = 4.4 minutes.
Step 4: conclusion — on a typical day **Café A is quicker** (median 4.5 compared with 7), but it is less reliable: once it took 26 minutes.

### Example 4

Liam's mean mark over 5 tests is 72. What must he score on the 6th test to lift his mean to 75?

Step 1: total so far = 72 × 5 = 360 — rebuild the total from the mean.
Step 2: total needed = 75 × 6 = 450 — 6 tests at a mean of 75.
Step 3: 6th test = 450 − 360 = **90**.
Check: (360 + 90) ÷ 6 = 450 ÷ 6 = 75 ✓

## Common mistakes

- **Comparing only the centre.** Two sets with the same mean can behave very differently. Fix: always give a centre AND a spread.
- **Reading the left side of a back-to-back plot backwards.** The leaf next to the stem is the smallest. Fix: read left leaves from the stem outwards.
- **Trusting a mean that has an outlier in it.** Fix: look at the plot first; if there is an outlier, use the median for "typical".
- **Comparing totals of groups of different sizes.** Fix: compare means or medians.
- **Adding means together.** The mean of two groups is not the average of their means unless the groups are the same size. Fix: rebuild each total with mean × number, add the totals, then divide by the total number.

## Tips to remember

- **"Centre AND spread, every time."** (A made-up memory trick.) Each comparison sentence needs one of each.
- **Same scale or no deal.** Two plots can only be compared by eye if they share the same scale.
- **Left leaves lean out.** On a back-to-back plot, the left leaves grow as they move away from the stem.
- **Mean × count = total.** Whenever a question gives you a mean and asks for something else, rebuild the total first.
- **Outlier? Median!** The median ignores one wild value; the mean and range do not.

## Key terms

- **Data set** — a collection of values about one group.
- **Measure of centre** — a single typical value: the mean, median or mode.
- **Range** — highest value minus lowest value; a simple measure of spread.
- **Consistent** — values that are close together (small spread).
- **Outlier** — a value much higher or lower than the rest.
- **Parallel dot plots** — two dot plots drawn on the same scale, one above the other.
- **Back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot** — two stem-and-leaf plots sharing one stem, one group on each side.

## Summary

- Compare data sets with a measure of centre and a measure of spread.
- Parallel dot plots and back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots show two groups on one scale.
- An outlier pulls the mean and range a long way but hardly moves the median.
- Compare means or medians, not totals, when groups are different sizes.
- total = mean × number of values lets you find missing or needed values.

questions.prompt: The parallel dot plots show the hours of sleep for 7 Year 7 students and 7 adults. How many hours greater is the median for the Year 7s than for the adults?
questions.explanation: The Year 7 median is 9 (the 4th of 8, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10, 10) and the adult median is 7 (the 4th of 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9), so the difference is 2 hours. Using the adults' mode (6) instead of the median gives 3, which is wrong.
steps: Each group has 7 values, so the median is the 4th value in order.
Year 7s in order: 8, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10, 10 → median 9. Adults: 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9 → median 7.
Difference = 9 − 7 = 2 hours.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 1 is the difference between the two ranges (3 − 2). The question asks about the medians.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 6 is the adults' mode (the most common value), not the median. The median is the 4th of the 7 values in order.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you added the two medians. "How many hours greater" means subtract.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of hours of sleep from 5 to 11. Year 7s: two dots at 8, three at 9, two at 10. Adults: three dots at 6, two at 7, one at 8 and one at 9.

questions.prompt: Class P and Class Q did the same quiz. Class P: mean 14, range 3. Class Q: mean 14, range 11. Which statement is the best comparison?

options.A: Class Q did better, because its range is bigger.
options.B: Class P did better, because its range is smaller.
options.C: The two classes performed identically, because their means are equal.
options.D: They did equally well on average, but Class P's scores were more consistent.

questions.explanation: The means are equal (14), so on average the classes did equally well; Class P's smaller range (3 compared with 11) means its scores were more bunched together. Saying the classes are identical ignores the spread.
steps: Compare the centres: both means are 14, so equal on average.
Compare the spreads: P's range is 3, Q's is 11, so P is more consistent.
Best statement: equal on average, but P is more consistent.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a bigger range does not mean higher scores — it means the scores are more spread out.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the means are equal, so neither class did better on average. A smaller range means more consistent, not better.
mistakes.C: Step 2: equal centres are only half the story — the ranges (3 and 11) are very different.

questions.prompt: Four numbers have a mean of 9. What is the total of the four numbers?
questions.explanation: Mean = total ÷ 4, so total = 9 × 4 = 36. Adding 9 + 4 = 13 does not undo a division.
steps: Mean = total ÷ number of values, so total = mean × number of values.

mistakes.B: Step 2: you added the mean and the count (9 + 4). Total = mean × number of values.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you divided 9 by 4. To rebuild the total, multiply the mean by the number of values.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 9 is the mean (the "fair share" each number gets), not the total of all four.

questions.prompt:
Sit-ups done in one minute:

| Year 7 leaves | Stem | Year 8 leaves |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 1 | |
| 7 5 2 | 2 | 4 9 |
| 8 4 3 1 | 3 | 2 5 6 8 |
| 1 | 4 | 0 2 5 |

Key: 2 | 4 means 24 for Year 8, and 5 | 2 means 25 for Year 7. How much higher is the Year 8 median than the Year 7 median?
questions.explanation: Year 7 in order: 18, 22, 25, 27, 31, 33, 34, 38, 41 (median 31). Year 8: 24, 29, 32, 35, 36, 38, 40, 42, 45 (median 36). 36 − 31 = 5. The answer 5.8 compares means, not medians.
steps: Read the left (Year 7) leaves from the stem outwards: 18, 22, 25, 27, 31, 33, 34, 38, 41 — the 5th of 9 is 31.
Difference = 36 − 31 = 5.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 2 is the difference between the ranges (23 − 21). The question asks about the medians.
mistakes.B: Step 3: about 5.8 is the difference between the means. Use the middle (5th) value of each group instead.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 38 is the 6th Year 8 value. With 9 values, the median is the 5th: 24, 29, 32, 35, 36.

questions.prompt: The dot plots show Set A and Set B. Set B has one value far from the others. Which value best describes a typical value in Set B?
questions.explanation: Set B is 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 21. The outlier 21 pulls the mean to 42 ÷ 7 = 6, above almost every value, while the median (4th value) is 4 — right in the middle of the bunch.
steps: Set B in order: 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 21. The value 21 is an outlier.
Mean = 42 ÷ 7 = 6, which is higher than six of the seven values — the outlier has dragged it up.
The median (4th value) is 4, which sits in the middle of the bunch, so the median, 4, is the best typical value.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the outlier 21 drags the mean up to 6, which is bigger than six of the seven values. Use the median when there is an outlier.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the range measures spread, not a typical value.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the question asks about Set B only. Read the lower row of dots.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots on a scale from 0 to 22. Set A: one dot at 5 and two dots each at 6, 7 and 8. Set B: one dot at 2, two at 3, two at 4, one at 5 and one far away at 21.

questions.prompt: Six scores have a mean of 15. One score, 9, is removed. What is the mean of the five scores that are left?
questions.explanation: Total = 15 × 6 = 90. Remove 9: 81. New mean = 81 ÷ 5 = 16.2. Dividing 81 by 6 forgets that one score has gone.
steps: Total of the six scores = 15 × 6 = 90.
Remove the 9: 90 − 9 = 81.
Five scores remain: 81 ÷ 5 = 16.2.

mistakes.B: Step 2: you divided the old total (90) by 5 without first removing the 9.
mistakes.C: Step 3: there are only 5 scores left, so divide 81 by 5, not by 6.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you subtracted 9 from the mean. Rebuild the total first: 15 × 6.

questions.prompt: Group A has 10 students with a mean mark of 70. Group B has 15 students with a mean mark of 80. What is the mean mark of all 25 students together?
questions.explanation: Totals: 10 × 70 = 700 and 15 × 80 = 1200, so 1900 ÷ 25 = 76. Averaging the means (75) ignores that Group B is bigger.
steps: Group A total = 10 × 70 = 700. Group B total = 15 × 80 = 1200.
Combined total = 700 + 1200 = 1900 marks.
Combined mean = 1900 ÷ 25 = 76.

mistakes.A: Step 3: you averaged the two means. Group B has more students, so its total counts for more — add the totals, then divide by 25.
mistakes.B: Step 1: you multiplied the wrong pairs (10 × 80 and 15 × 70). Group A has 10 students at 70.
mistakes.C: Step 3: divide the combined total by the number of students (25), not by the number of groups (2).

questions.prompt: The dot plots show 8 travel times to school by train and 8 by bus. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The bus has a lower median, because its fastest trip (10 minutes) is quicker.
options.B: The train has a larger range, because it has more dots stacked up.
options.C: The train has a lower median and a smaller range.
options.D: Both have the same median, because both have a dot at 16.

questions.explanation: Train: median (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = 15.5, range 18 − 12 = 6. Bus: median (16 + 19) ÷ 2 = 17.5, range 25 − 10 = 15. So the train is quicker in the middle and more consistent.
steps: Medians (average of 4th and 5th values): train (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = 15.5; bus (16 + 19) ÷ 2 = 17.5.
Ranges: train 18 − 12 = 6; bus 25 − 10 = 15.
So the train has the lower median and the smaller range.

mistakes.A: Step 1: one fast trip does not set the median. The bus median is (16 + 19) ÷ 2 = 17.5.
mistakes.B: Step 2: stacked dots mean values are bunched, so the range is smaller. Range = highest − lowest.
mistakes.D: Step 1: with 8 values the median is the average of the 4th and 5th values in order, which are different for the two groups.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of travel time from 10 to 26 minutes. Train: dots at 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 16, 16 and 18. Bus: dots at 10, 11, 13, 16, 19, 20, 22 and 25.

questions.prompt: The data set is 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 18, 19, 48. The outlier 48 is removed. What happens to the mean and the median?

options.A: The mean falls by 4 and the median falls by 1.
options.B: The mean falls by 6 and the median falls by 1.
options.C: The mean falls by 4 and the median does not change.
options.D: The mean falls by 1 and the median falls by 4.

questions.explanation: Before: mean 160 ÷ 8 = 20, median (16 + 18) ÷ 2 = 17. After: mean 112 ÷ 7 = 16, median = 4th of 7 = 16. Mean falls by 4, median by only 1 — the median barely notices outliers.
steps: Before: total 160, mean 160 ÷ 8 = 20; median = (16 + 18) ÷ 2 = 17.
After removing 48: total 112, mean 112 ÷ 7 = 16 — a fall of 4.
New median = 4th of 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 18, 19 = 16 — a fall of 1.

mistakes.B: Step 2: you took 48 ÷ 8 = 6 off the mean. Work out the new mean properly: 112 ÷ 7.
mistakes.C: Step 3: the median does move a little — with 7 values it becomes the 4th value, not the average of two middle values.
mistakes.D: Steps 2 and 3: you swapped them. The outlier changes the mean a lot and the median only a little.

questions.prompt: Five whole numbers have a mean of 8, a median of 9, a mode of 10 and a range of 6. What is the smallest of the five numbers?
questions.explanation: In order the numbers are _, _, 9, 10, 10 (the mode needs two 10s above the median). Range 6 makes the smallest 10 − 6 = 4, and the total 40 makes the other 7: 4, 7, 9, 10, 10. Using 7 as the answer picks the wrong position.
steps: Write them in order: a, b, 9, d, e — the median is the middle one.
The mode is 10, so 10 appears at least twice; it must be d and e (both are at least 9). So the list is a, b, 9, 10, 10.
Mean 8 means the total is 40, so a + b = 40 − 29 = 11.
Range 6: a = 10 − 6 = 4 (and then b = 7). The smallest number is 4.

mistakes.A: Step 4: 7 is the second-smallest number. The smallest is found from the range: largest − 6.
mistakes.B: Step 4: the range is measured from the largest number (10), not from the mean (8).
mistakes.C: Step 4: the range is measured from the largest number (10), not from the median (9).

questions.prompt: A class of 24 students has a mean test mark of 70. A new student sits the test, and the class mean rises to exactly 71. What mark did the new student get?
questions.explanation: Old total 70 × 24 = 1680; new total 71 × 25 = 1775; new mark = 1775 − 1680 = 95. The new student had to lift all 25 people's mean by 1, so they needed 70 + 25 = 95, not 94.
steps: Old total = 70 × 24 = 1680.
New total (25 students) = 71 × 25 = 1775.
New student's mark = 1775 − 1680 = 95.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 71 is the new mean. A mark of 71 would barely move the mean — rebuild both totals.
mistakes.C: Step 2: there are now 25 students, so the new total is 71 × 25, not 71 × 24 + 70.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 1775 is the new class total. Subtract the old total (1680) to find the new mark.

questions.prompt: The dot plots show the goals Ana and Ben scored in 9 games each. Ben plays one more game. How many goals must he score in it so that his mean over 10 games equals Ana's mean over her 9 games?
questions.explanation: Ana: 54 ÷ 9 = 6. Ben needs 10 × 6 = 60 goals in 10 games and has 45, so he needs 15. The tempting 9 forgets that Ben's mean is over 10 games, not 9.
steps: For a mean of 6 over 10 games Ben needs 10 × 6 = 60 goals, so 60 − 45 = 15 in the last game.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 6 is Ana's mean. Ben is behind, so scoring only 6 would leave his mean below 6.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 9 is the gap between the two totals (54 − 45), but Ben's 10 games need a total of 60, not 54.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 60 is the total Ben needs over all 10 games. Subtract the 45 he already has.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of goals per game from 0 to 10. Ana: one dot at 4, two at 5, three at 6, two at 7, one at 8. Ben: one at 2, one at 3, two at 4, two at 5, one at 6, one at 7, one at 9.
